meta.title: Backlog: Epics and Features, in plain language
meta.eyebrow: Epic and Feature · review before the tracker · fictional example
meta.lede: The whole backlog of the Broker Assistant in one document, written so that a developer, a QA and a sales manager read the same thing. Codes, scope, dependencies and rules are the tracker's; the writing is plain. Everything here is fictional: the brokerage, the people, the numbers and the dates.
meta.how_to_read: "Write to the CRM" means updating a field in the brokerage's CRM after the broker approves. "Wave" (ondas, in the vocabulary this layout comes from) is a delivery group that ends with something a broker uses. "Points" are Fibonacci story points set by the developer who will build the story.
meta.footer: Fictional program for a fictional brokerage. Generated from tools/backlog_document/acme_realty_backlog.json by build.py; do not edit the HTML by hand. Part of the Backlog Writing System.
meta.export_note: In the original, this chapter writes owner, points and sprint to Azure DevOps from the browser, with a token that lives only in the open tab. This public version exports the plan instead.

waves.name: Leads and approval
waves.title: Wave 1 · Leads and approval: the lead is answered and every write is approved
waves.usable: The broker opens one queue with every portal lead, its listing facts and the open questions; a drafted first reply goes out after approval; every write to the CRM is previewed field by field, can be undone for a day, and shows up in the evening digest. The first three Features are the MVP and depend on no outside access.
waves.not_covered: Qualification happens in the broker's head for now; visits and proposals are still recorded by hand.

waves.name: Visits
waves.title: Wave 2 · Visits: a prepared broker and a recorded outcome
waves.usable: A one-page sheet before the visit, three fitting slots proposed in the conversation, and the outcome spoken in the car and proposed as fields. Qualification questions run in the conversation and a score the broker can explain orders the queue.
waves.not_covered: Proposals and the forecast still live outside the assistant.

waves.name: Proposals
waves.title: Wave 3 · Proposals: nothing stays silent
waves.usable: Every proposal has a next step and a date; the follow-up is drafted on the date; counter-proposals are checked against the developer's table before they leave; brokers switch capabilities to always-allow at their own pace.
waves.not_covered: The developer's answers still arrive by phone until the parallel track lands.

waves.name: Forecast
waves.title: Wave 4 · Forecast: the stage and the category read the evidence
waves.usable: The stage is proposed from the last event with its rule; the category from stage, score and status; the manager's Monday view shows reasons, disagreements and month-end accuracy.
waves.not_covered: Revenue projections and automatic stage writes stay out until the rules have two scored months.

waves.name: Parallel track
waves.title: Parallel track · Developer status sync
waves.usable: The two developers' daily exports are imported and matched, status changes are proposed to the broker, and the sync is measured weekly. It runs beside waves 3 and 4 because it depends on an access agreement, not on the waves.
waves.not_covered: Developer APIs and the other developers.

sprints.name: Sprint 3
sprints.note: Closed with 10 stories and 40 points of the 42 planned (illustrative).

sprints.name: Sprint 5
sprints.note: Planned in this document, in the review meeting, before anything is loaded into the tracker.

epics.name: Leads become qualified conversations
epics.summary: A lead from a property portal reaches the broker with context and a drafted first reply, instead of a bare name and phone number.

features.name: The lead queue with context
features.summary: The broker opens one queue where every portal lead shows the listing, the buyer's message and what is still unknown.

kpi.name: First reply within one hour
kpi.definition: Leads answered within 60 minutes of arrival ÷ leads received in the period
kpi.impact: A lead answered in the first hour is the one that converts; this queue is where the hour starts.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Receive portal leads into one queue
stories.summary: A lead sent by a portal appears in the broker's queue within a minute, with the portal, the listing and the buyer's message.

sections.why: Today a lead is an email the broker may read tonight. If the queue does not exist, nothing else in the program has a starting point.
sections.context: Three portals send leads by email in three formats; the brokerage also receives walk-in leads typed by the reception.
sections.story: As a broker, I want every portal lead in one queue with its listing and message, so that I answer from one place instead of three inboxes.
expected: The lead record shows portal, listing code, buyer name, phone, email and the message as written.
Arrival time and the time since arrival are visible on the row.
A lead for a listing the broker does not handle is routed to the listing's broker.
out: Portal APIs; this story parses emails and imports CSV.
tech: Email parser per portal with a test fixture per format.
Duplicate check by phone and email across the last 30 days.
trace: Program brief section 2; portal export formats, read on 2026-02-20.

cases.case: A portal lead lands in the queue
cases.given: a portal sends a lead email for listing AR-2041
cases.then: the lead is in the broker's queue within one minute with portal, listing and message.

cases.given: the same phone number wrote through two portals in the same week
cases.then: the queue shows one lead with both portals listed, not two leads.

cases.case: A lead for another broker's listing
cases.given: the listing belongs to a different broker
cases.then: it lands in that broker's queue and the first broker does not see it.

stories.name: Show what is still unknown about the buyer
stories.summary: Next to each lead the broker sees the questions nobody has answered yet: budget, financing, timing, must-haves.

sections.why: A broker who calls without knowing what to ask repeats the portal form. The open questions turn the first call into qualification.
sections.context: The portal form rarely carries budget or financing; the buyer's message sometimes does.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to see which qualification facts are missing, so that my first call covers them.
expected: Four facts tracked: budget range, financing status, moving timeline, must-haves.
Facts found in the message are filled with the sentence they came from.
Missing facts are listed as questions in the broker's words.
tech: Extraction from the message text with a confidence flag; low confidence shows as unknown, never as a guess.
trace: Qualification checklist agreed with the sales manager on 2026-02-27.

cases.case: A budget found in the message
cases.given: the buyer wrote 'up to 900 thousand'
cases.then: budget shows 'up to 900 thousand' with the phrase next to it.

cases.case: A fact that is not there
cases.given: the message says nothing about financing
cases.then: financing is listed under 'still to ask', not filled with a guess.

stories.name: Attach the listing facts the buyer will ask about
stories.summary: The lead shows the listing's price, size, floor, parking and the developer's current conditions, from the catalogue.

sections.why: Brokers answer price and conditions from memory and get them wrong when a developer changes a campaign. The catalogue is the source; the lead should read it.
sections.context: The brokerage keeps a catalogue with the developer's conditions, updated weekly by the back office.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the listing facts next to the lead, so that my first reply is right without opening the catalogue.
expected: Price, area, floor, parking, delivery date and current campaign conditions shown with the catalogue's update date.
A listing with no catalogue entry shows 'not in the catalogue' and a link to request it.
tech: Read-only query to the catalogue by listing code.

cases.case: The facts come from the catalogue
cases.given: listing AR-2041 is in the catalogue with conditions dated last Friday
cases.then: price, area, floor, parking, delivery and conditions appear with that date.

cases.given: listing AR-7788 is not in the catalogue
cases.then: the lead says 'not in the catalogue' and offers the request link; nothing is invented.

stories.name: Flag leads that are waiting too long
stories.summary: A lead with no reply after 30 minutes is highlighted, and the manager sees the count per broker.

sections.why: The hour is lost in silence. A visible timer and a count per broker make the delay a shared fact instead of a private one.
sections.context: Brokers are often at visits; the manager redistributes by hand today.
sections.story: As a sales manager, I want to see leads waiting past 30 minutes per broker, so that I redistribute before the hour is lost.
expected: Rows turn amber at 30 minutes and red at 60.
The manager's view counts waiting leads per broker.
Redistribution is a manual action by the manager with a reason.
tech: Timer from arrival time; the manager's view reads the same records.

cases.given: a lead arrived 31 minutes ago with no reply
cases.then: the row is amber and counts in the manager's view.

cases.given: the manager moves the lead to another broker with a reason
cases.then: the lead appears in the new queue, and the trail records who moved it and why.

sections.why: Nothing in the program starts before the lead is in one place with its context. This Feature is the queue and the context; the reply and the qualification build on it.
sections.problem: Leads arrive by email from three portals in three formats and are copied by hand, late, into the CRM.
sections.objective: Every lead in one queue within a minute, with the listing facts and the open questions, and a visible timer.
sections.value: The first hour becomes visible and manageable; the first reply (F02) has something to say.
behavior: One queue per broker, ordered by arrival.
Listing facts from the catalogue, dated.
Timer and manager's count of waiting leads.
acceptance: A portal lead is in the queue within one minute of the email.
Listing facts carry the catalogue date.
A lead past 30 minutes is highlighted and counted.
scope: In: three portals by email, CSV import, catalogue read.
rules: A lead belongs to the listing's broker.
Nothing is guessed: a missing fact is a question.
data: Portal emails (source of truth for the lead).
Catalogue (source of truth for listing facts).
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Parser accuracy per portal on a 40-email golden set: 100% on required fields (illustrative).
Extraction of the four facts: no guessed value in the never-cases.
open: Whether reception-typed leads enter through the same queue (decision by 2026-04-20).

features.name: The first reply, drafted and sent after approval
features.summary: The assistant drafts the first reply to a lead from the listing facts and the buyer's message; the broker edits, approves and it goes out.

kpi.name: First reply within one hour
kpi.definition: Leads answered within 60 minutes of arrival ÷ leads received in the period
kpi.impact: This Feature is the reply itself; it exists to move the first-hour number.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Draft the first reply from the lead and the listing
stories.summary: For each new lead the assistant drafts a reply that answers what the buyer asked, with the listing facts, and asks one qualification question.

sections.why: The broker writes the same reply forty times a month from memory. A draft that already has the facts turns a ten-minute task into a one-minute review.
sections.context: Replies go by WhatsApp or email depending on the portal; tone is the brokerage's, short and concrete.
sections.story: As a broker, I want a drafted reply that answers the buyer and asks one question, so that I only review and send.
expected: The draft answers each question in the buyer's message with a catalogue fact or says the broker will confirm.
Exactly one qualification question from the open list.
The draft is stored until the broker approves or discards it.
tech: Model call with the listing facts and the message as context; the draft shows which fact each sentence used.

cases.case: A draft answers the question asked
cases.given: the buyer asked about parking
cases.then: it states the parking from the catalogue and asks one open question.

cases.case: A fact not in the catalogue
cases.given: the buyer asked about the condominium fee and the catalogue has none
cases.then: the draft says the broker will confirm the fee; it never states a number.

cases.given: the buyer asked for a discount
cases.then: the draft contains no discount or condition absent from the catalogue.

stories.name: Edit, approve and send the reply from the queue
stories.summary: The broker edits the draft in place, approves, and the reply is sent through the lead's channel from the broker's own identity.

sections.why: A draft that has to be copied into another app is a draft nobody uses.
sections.context: WhatsApp through the brokerage's business account; email through the broker's mailbox.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to approve and send from the queue, so that the reply leaves in one click.
expected: Approve sends; discard records the reason; edit keeps the original for comparison.
The sent reply is written to the lead's timeline with the time.
tech: Channel adapters for WhatsApp business and email; the send is logged as a write through the single write path.

cases.case: Approve sends through the right channel
cases.given: the lead came from a portal that provides a phone number
cases.then: the reply goes by WhatsApp from the brokerage account and appears on the timeline.

cases.given: the broker discards the draft
cases.then: the reason is stored and the lead stays in the queue as unanswered.

stories.name: Learn from the broker's edits
stories.summary: Edits made before approval are kept and summarized so the next drafts for the same broker get closer to how they write.

sections.why: If the draft never improves, the broker stops editing and starts rewriting, and the time saving is gone.
sections.context: Edits are small and repeated: greeting, closing, how prices are written.
sections.story: As a product manager, I want the edits measured and fed back, so that drafts improve and I can prove it.
expected: Edit distance per draft stored.
A weekly eval run on the golden set reports the share of drafts approved without edits.
Style notes per broker derived from repeated edits, shown to the broker and editable.
tech: Golden set of 40 leads with approved replies; rubric: answers the question, one question asked, tone, no invented fact.
trace: Eval plan, section 3 of the spec.

cases.given: a week of drafts has been approved or edited
cases.then: the report shows the share approved without edits and the edit distance median.

cases.given: the broker changed the closing in five of five drafts
cases.then: the style note 'closing: ...' is proposed to the broker, who can accept or delete it.

sections.why: The queue shows the lead; this Feature answers it. It is the single largest time saving in the Epic and the first place the brokers will judge the assistant.
sections.problem: Replies are written from memory, late, and repeat the portal form.
sections.objective: A reviewed reply out within the hour for 80% of leads.
sections.value: The broker's ten minutes become one; the buyer gets a specific answer while still interested.
behavior: Draft from the message and the catalogue.
Edit, approve, send from the queue.
acceptance: Each question in the message is answered or marked to confirm.
No fact absent from the catalogue.
rules: Tier 2 autonomy: approve each.
Never a price or condition that is not in the catalogue.
data: Lead record, catalogue, reply tone guide.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Golden set of 40 leads: 90% of drafts pass the rubric before the pilot; never-cases (invented fact, discount) at zero (illustrative).
open: Whether a draft may propose a visit slot in the first reply (decision with BA-VISIT-F03).

features.name: Qualification questions and a score
features.summary: After the first reply, the assistant asks the remaining qualification questions in the conversation and keeps a score the broker can read.

kpi.name: Qualified before the first visit
kpi.definition: Leads with the four facts known before the first visit ÷ leads that had a visit
kpi.impact: A qualified lead visits the right unit; an unqualified one visits three.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Ask the open questions one at a time
stories.summary: When the buyer replies, the assistant drafts the next message with the next open question, until the four facts are known.

sections.why: Asking four questions at once reads like a form; one at a time reads like a broker.
sections.context: The conversation runs on WhatsApp; the broker approves each message in the first release.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the next question drafted when the buyer answers, so that qualification happens in the conversation.
expected: Next question chosen from the open list in a fixed order: timing, budget, financing, must-haves.
The buyer's answer is proposed as the fact, with the phrase, for approval.
No question is repeated.
tech: Conversation state per lead; each proposed fact is a write through BA-CRM-F01.

cases.case: The next question follows the order
cases.given: timing is known and budget is not
cases.then: the draft asks the budget question only.

cases.case: An answer becomes a proposed fact
cases.given: the buyer wrote 'we have the financing approved'
cases.then: financing is proposed as 'approved' with the phrase, for the broker to approve.

stories.name: Keep a qualification score the broker can explain
stories.summary: Each lead shows a score from 0 to 4, one point per known fact that fits the listing, with the reason per point.

sections.why: A score nobody can explain is a score nobody trusts. Four facts, four points, each with its reason.
sections.context: The sales manager wants to prioritize visits by score.
sections.story: As a broker, I want a score I can explain to the manager, so that visit priority is not a gut feeling.
expected: Score = number of facts known and compatible with the listing.
Each point shows its reason; an incompatible fact shows why.
The score sorts the queue when the broker chooses.
tech: Rule-based; no model.

cases.given: budget 'up to 900 thousand' and the listing costs 850 thousand
cases.then: budget counts one point with the reason 'within budget'.

cases.given: the buyer needs delivery this year and the listing delivers in two years
cases.then: timing counts zero with the reason shown, and the lead is not hidden.

stories.name: Suggest a better-fitting listing when the facts do not match
stories.summary: When two or more facts do not fit the listing, the assistant proposes up to three listings from the catalogue that do.

sections.why: A lead that does not fit the listing is not a lost lead; it is a lead for another listing. Today it is lost.
sections.context: The catalogue has the facts needed to match budget, timing and must-haves.
sections.story: As a broker, I want alternatives proposed when the fit is poor, so that I keep the buyer instead of the listing.
expected: Up to three alternatives with the matching facts shown.
The broker picks one or none; the pick is written as the lead's listing with the previous one kept.
No alternative is sent to the buyer without approval.
tech: Catalogue query by budget band, delivery date and must-haves.

cases.given: budget and timing do not fit the listing
cases.then: up to three listings appear with the facts that match, and the original listing stays.

cases.given: nothing in the catalogue fits the budget
cases.then: the assistant says so; it does not stretch the budget.

sections.why: A first reply opens a conversation; this Feature turns the conversation into four facts and a score. Without it, qualification stays in the broker's head.
sections.problem: Brokers visit with unqualified buyers and the manager cannot prioritize.
sections.objective: The four facts known before the first visit for 70% of leads, with a score the broker can explain.
sections.value: Fewer wasted visits; the right listing for the buyer.
behavior: One question at a time in the conversation.
A score of 0 to 4 with reasons.
Alternatives when the fit is poor.
acceptance: Each score point has a reason.
Alternatives come from the catalogue only.
rules: Rules, not a model, for the score.
Nothing sent without approval.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Score agreement with the sales manager's manual score on 30 leads: 90% (illustrative).
open: Whether the score is shown to the buyer's broker only or also to the manager in real time.

sections.why: A brokerage receives hundreds of portal leads a month and most die in the first hour: the broker is at a visit, the reply comes late, and the buyer has already written to three other brokers. Without this Epic the assistant has nothing to work with: no queue, no context, no first reply.
sections.problem: Portal leads arrive by email and in three portal back offices. Brokers copy them by hand into the CRM, reply from memory, and lose the ones that arrive during visits.
sections.objective: Every lead is in the broker's queue within a minute, with the listing, the buyer's message and the questions the broker still has to ask, and the first reply goes out the same hour after the broker approves it.
metrics: First reply within one hour, from 35% to 80% of leads (illustrative).
Leads with a qualification score before the first visit: 70%.
Portal leads lost to a late reply, read from the portal's own report: half of today's number.
scope: The drafted first reply, sent after approval (BA-LEAD-F02).
rules: The assistant never contacts a buyer without the broker's approval.
A lead belongs to one broker; redistribution is the manager's decision, not the assistant's.
The portal of origin and its lead id stay on the record.
sections.dependencies: Portal exports (email and CSV) in wave 1; portal APIs are a later enabler. BA-CRM-F01 for any write to the CRM.
risks: Risk: a portal changes its email format and leads stop arriving. Mitigation: a daily count per portal with an alert when it drops to zero.
Risk: the drafted reply sounds generic. Mitigation: the broker edits before approving, and edits feed the next drafts.
Risk: duplicate leads across portals. Mitigation: match by phone and email before creating a record.
governance: The sales manager owns the queue rules and the redistribution.
Weekly reading of first-reply time per broker in the manager's digest.
Autonomy: the assistant drafts; sending stays at tier 2 (approve each) in the first release.
technical: Inbound: portal emails parsed into a lead record; CSV import as a fallback.
Listing data from the brokerage's catalogue, read only.
Reads and writes go through the assistant's single CRM write path; every write carries author, previous value, proposed value, written value, origin and approval.
sections.estimate: 11 User Stories, 34 points estimated by the developers (illustrative).

epics.name: Every visit has a prepared broker and a recorded outcome
epics.summary: Before a visit the broker knows the unit, the price, the buyer's answers and what is still open; after it, the outcome is in the CRM without typing.

features.name: The visit preparation sheet
features.summary: Before a visit, one page shows the unit, the price and conditions, the buyer's facts and what the broker still has to find out.

kpi.name: Visits prepared
kpi.definition: Visits whose sheet was opened before the visit ÷ visits held
kpi.impact: A prepared broker closes the second visit during the first one.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Build the sheet from the lead and the catalogue
stories.summary: The sheet assembles the unit facts, the campaign conditions, the buyer's four facts and the open questions, on one phone screen.

sections.why: The broker prepares from PDFs in a chat thread; one page beats five attachments.
sections.context: Visits are confirmed the day before; the sheet is read in the car.
sections.story: As a broker, I want one page with everything I need for the visit, so that I walk in prepared.
expected: Unit facts, conditions with date, buyer facts, open questions, last conversation.
Readable on a phone, offline once opened.
tech: Server-rendered page cached on the device.

cases.case: The sheet has the four blocks
cases.given: a visit is scheduled for listing AR-2041 with lead 1180
cases.then: it shows unit facts, conditions dated, the buyer's facts and the open questions.

cases.given: the sheet was opened once with network
cases.when: the broker opens it in the car without network
cases.then: the sheet is readable.

stories.name: Compare with two similar units
stories.summary: The sheet shows two comparable units from the catalogue with price per square meter, so the broker can answer 'is this expensive'.

sections.why: The first objection at a visit is the price; a comparison on the sheet answers it with facts.
sections.context: Comparables by area band, neighborhood and delivery date.
sections.story: As a broker, I want two comparables on the sheet, so that I answer the price objection with numbers.
expected: Two units from the same neighborhood and area band, price per square meter shown.
The comparables' dates shown; no comparable older than 60 days.
tech: Catalogue query; price per square meter computed from price and private area.

cases.given: the catalogue has three units in the band
cases.then: two appear with price per square meter and dates.

cases.given: all candidates are older than 60 days
cases.then: the block says 'no recent comparable' instead of showing stale ones.

stories.name: Remind the broker of the sheet before the visit
stories.summary: Two hours before a visit the broker receives the sheet link; opening it is recorded for the KPI.

sections.why: A sheet that is not opened does not prepare anyone, and the KPI needs the opening to be a fact.
sections.context: Reminders by WhatsApp to the broker, not the buyer.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the sheet sent before the visit, so that I do not have to look for it.
expected: Reminder two hours before, with the link.
Opening is logged with time and device.
tech: Scheduled job from the visit time; open event through the single write path as an activity.

cases.given: a visit is at 15:00
cases.then: the broker receives the link and the sheet is one tap away.

cases.given: the broker opens the sheet
cases.then: the activity 'sheet opened' is written with the time.

sections.why: The visit is the most expensive hour of the sale and today it starts from memory. The sheet puts the facts in the broker's hand before the door opens.
sections.problem: Scattered PDFs, no comparables, no record that the broker prepared.
sections.objective: A sheet opened before 85% of visits.
sections.value: Fewer wrong answers at the door; the price objection answered with numbers.
behavior: One page from lead and catalogue.
A reminder with the link, and the opening recorded.
rules: Only catalogue facts.
No comparable older than 60 days.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Sheets opened before the visit, read weekly.
open: Whether the sheet may show the developer's internal discount band (commercial director's decision).

features.name: Visit outcome by voice or text
features.summary: After the visit the broker speaks or types what happened and the assistant proposes the fields: interest, objections, next step, date.

kpi.name: Outcome recorded within an hour
kpi.definition: Visits with an outcome recorded within 60 minutes ÷ visits held
kpi.impact: The outcome is what the forecast and the follow-up read; without it both read nothing.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Turn a voice note into proposed fields
stories.summary: The broker records a voice note after the visit; the assistant transcribes it and proposes interest level, objections, next step and date, each with the phrase it came from.

sections.why: The outcome is spoken in the car and typed never. Voice is the only channel that will be used within the hour.
sections.context: Transcription in Portuguese; fields in the CRM's vocabulary.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to say what happened and see the fields proposed, so that the CRM is updated before I reach the next visit.
expected: Transcript kept as evidence.
Four fields proposed, each with the source phrase.
Amounts and dates shown next to the phrase; unclear values proposed as unknown.
tech: Speech to text, then field extraction; the preview is BA-CRM-F01's.
trace: Program brief section 6; CRM field list.

cases.given: the broker said 'they liked it, worried about the fee, will decide by Friday'
cases.then: interest high, objection 'condominium fee', next step 'decision', date Friday, each with its phrase.

cases.given: the broker said 'maybe around eight something'
cases.then: no amount is proposed; the field says unknown with the phrase.

stories.name: Type the outcome when voice is not possible
stories.summary: The same four fields can be filled from a short typed message, with the same preview.

sections.why: In a developer's stand the broker cannot record; typing must produce the same result.
sections.context: Text through the assistant's chat.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to type the outcome when I cannot speak, so that nothing waits for the office.
expected: Same extraction and preview as the voice path.
A message with no outcome content asks one question back.
tech: Shared extraction; channel adapter for text.

cases.given: the broker typed 'liked it, fee objection, decides Friday'
cases.then: the same four fields are proposed as from voice.

cases.given: the broker typed 'visit done'
cases.then: the assistant asks what the buyer said, and proposes nothing.

stories.name: Block the stage change without an outcome
stories.summary: A deal cannot move to the next stage while its last visit has no recorded outcome; the broker is told what is missing.

sections.why: Stages move on hope; the outcome is the evidence. The block is what makes the forecast read evidence.
sections.context: Stage changes happen in the CRM and through the assistant.
sections.story: As a sales manager, I want stage changes blocked without an outcome, so that the pipeline reads what happened.
expected: Block with the reason and a link to record the outcome.
The manager can override with a reason, recorded.
tech: Rule in the write path for the stage field.

cases.given: the last visit has no outcome
cases.then: the move is refused with 'record the outcome of the visit on April 2' and a link.

cases.given: the manager moves the stage with a reason
cases.then: the stage changes and the trail shows the override and the reason.

sections.why: The visit outcome is the fact every later step depends on. Spoken in the car, it reaches the CRM; typed tonight, it does not.
sections.problem: Outcomes recorded hours later or never; stages moved without evidence.
sections.objective: An outcome within the hour for 90% of visits.
sections.value: A pipeline that reads what happened; follow-ups that start on time.
behavior: Voice note to proposed fields with phrases.
Stage change blocked without an outcome.
acceptance: Each proposed field has its phrase.
Unclear values are unknown, never guessed.
The block names what is missing.
scope: Out: free-form notes, automatic stage change.
rules: Tier 2 for all four fields in the first release.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Golden set of 30 voice notes: field accuracy 90%, never-cases (invented amount) zero (illustrative).
open: Whether the transcript is stored for 30 or 90 days (legal decision).

features.name: Scheduling with the buyer and the developer's stand
features.summary: The assistant proposes visit slots that fit the broker's calendar and the stand's hours, and confirms with the buyer after approval.

kpi.name: Visits scheduled from the conversation
kpi.definition: Visits scheduled by the assistant ÷ visits held
kpi.impact: A slot offered in the conversation becomes a visit; a 'let me check' becomes silence.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Offer three slots that fit everyone
stories.summary: When a buyer agrees to visit, the assistant drafts a message with three slots that fit the broker's calendar and the stand's hours.

sections.why: Scheduling by message takes five exchanges; three fitting slots take one.
sections.context: The brokerage calendar is the broker's; stands have fixed hours per listing in the catalogue.
sections.story: As a broker, I want three fitting slots drafted, so that scheduling takes one message.
expected: Slots from the next three days, inside stand hours, outside the broker's busy times.
Travel time between visits respected (30 minutes default).
The draft goes out after approval.
tech: Calendar free-busy read; stand hours from the catalogue.

cases.given: the stand opens 10:00 to 18:00
cases.then: none is outside those hours.

cases.given: the broker has a visit at 14:00
cases.then: none starts between 13:30 and 15:00.

stories.name: Confirm and write the visit to both calendars
stories.summary: When the buyer picks a slot, the visit is written to the broker's calendar and the CRM, and the buyer gets a confirmation with the address.

sections.why: A visit that is not in the calendar is a visit the broker forgets.
sections.context: Confirmation by the same channel as the conversation.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the picked slot written everywhere, so that I never double-book.
expected: Calendar event with address and buyer facts.
CRM visit record through the single write path.
Confirmation message after the broker's approval.
tech: Calendar write; CRM write; channel send.

cases.given: the buyer replied 'Tuesday 11:00'
cases.then: the calendar has the event, the CRM has the visit, and the buyer receives the confirmation.

cases.case: The slot is no longer free
cases.given: another visit took Tuesday 11:00 meanwhile
cases.then: the assistant says the slot is gone and offers the next two.

stories.name: Remind the buyer the day before
stories.summary: The buyer receives a reminder with the address and the broker's name the day before, after the broker's approval or automatically once the capability is on always-allow.

sections.why: No-shows are the silent cost of visits; a reminder cuts them.
sections.context: Reminders are the first capability the brokers will want on always-allow.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the buyer reminded the day before, so that fewer visits are no-shows.
expected: Reminder at 18:00 the day before with address and name.
Tier 2 by default; tier 3 when the broker switches always-allow (BA-CRM-F02).
tech: Scheduled send; always-allow checked at send time.

cases.given: always-allow is off
cases.then: the broker sees the reminder to approve; nothing is sent before.

cases.given: the broker switched reminders to always-allow
cases.then: the reminder is sent and logged with 'always-allow' as the approval.

sections.why: A buyer who agrees to visit has to be given a time in the same message, or the agreement cools. This Feature closes the loop from reply to visit.
sections.problem: Five messages to find a time; double bookings; no-shows.
sections.objective: 60% of visits scheduled by the assistant, written to both calendars.
sections.value: More visits from the same leads; fewer no-shows.
behavior: Written to calendar and CRM on pick.
acceptance: Slots inside stand hours and outside busy times.
rules: Nothing sent without approval unless always-allow is on for the capability.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Share of proposed slots accepted; no-show rate before and after.

sections.why: A visit is the most expensive moment of the sale and today it starts from memory and ends in a WhatsApp message that nobody records. Without this Epic the CRM shows visits that happened with no outcome, and the forecast reads a pipeline that does not exist.
sections.problem: Brokers prepare visits from scattered PDFs and chat threads, and record outcomes hours later, if at all. The manager cannot tell a cold visit from a hot one.
sections.objective: A one-page preparation before every visit and a recorded outcome within an hour after it, for 90% of visits.
metrics: Visits with a recorded outcome within one hour: from 30% to 90% (illustrative).
Visits with a preparation sheet opened before the visit: 85%.
Second visits scheduled during the first visit: a measured baseline, then plus 20%.
scope: Scheduling with the buyer and the developer's sales stand (BA-VISIT-F03).
Outcome capture by voice or text (BA-VISIT-F02).
rules: The outcome fields the assistant proposes are previewed and approved field by field (BA-CRM-F01).
A visit without a recorded outcome blocks the stage change in the forecast.
sections.dependencies: BA-LEAD-F01 for the buyer's context; BA-CRM-F01 for the writes; the developer's visit calendar for BA-VISIT-F03.
risks: Risk: voice capture misreads amounts. Mitigation: amounts are shown next to the source phrase and never written without approval.
Risk: developers' stands keep their own calendars. Mitigation: scheduling starts with the brokerage's own calendar and adds stands one by one.
governance: The sales manager reads visits without outcome in the weekly digest.
Autonomy: tier 2 for all writes in the first release; tier 3 for the visit date once the eval set passes.
technical: Calendar read and write through the brokerage's calendar provider.
Voice notes transcribed, then mapped to fields; the transcript is kept as evidence.
Reads and writes go through the assistant's single CRM write path; every write carries author, previous value, proposed value, written value, origin and approval.

epics.name: Proposals are followed up on time
epics.summary: A proposal never sits silent: the broker is reminded, the follow-up is drafted, and the developer's answer reaches the CRM.

features.name: Follow-up reminders and drafts
features.summary: When a proposal's next-step date arrives, the broker gets a drafted follow-up for the buyer or the developer, with the proposal facts.

kpi.name: Silent proposals
kpi.definition: Open proposals with no activity for seven days ÷ open proposals
kpi.impact: A silent proposal is a sale someone else closes.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Set a next step and a date on every proposal
stories.summary: A proposal cannot be saved without a next step and a date; the assistant proposes both from the outcome of the visit.

sections.why: A proposal without a next step is the definition of silence.
sections.context: Proposals are created after a visit, from the outcome.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the next step and date proposed when I create the proposal, so that no proposal is born silent.
expected: Next step from a fixed list: buyer decision, developer answer, document, counter-proposal.
Date proposed from the buyer's phrase or three working days by default.
Saved through the preview.
tech: Field rules in the write path.

cases.case: The proposal gets a step and a date
cases.given: the visit outcome said 'decides Friday'
cases.then: next step 'buyer decision', date Friday, both in the preview.

cases.given: the outcome has no date
cases.then: next step 'buyer decision', date in three working days, flagged as default.

stories.name: Draft the follow-up when the date arrives
stories.summary: On the date, the broker receives a drafted message for the buyer or the developer, with the proposal's facts and the question to ask.

sections.why: The reminder alone is ignored; the drafted message is sent.
sections.context: Buyer follow-ups by WhatsApp; developer follow-ups by email.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the follow-up drafted on the date, so that I send instead of writing.
expected: Draft with unit, value, date of the proposal and the one question.
Approve sends; snooze moves the date with a reason.
tech: Scheduled job; draft through the model with the proposal facts; send through the channel adapter.

cases.given: the next step is 'buyer decision' and the date is today
cases.then: the broker has a drafted message with the unit, the value and the question.

cases.given: the broker snoozes for two days with a reason
cases.then: the date moves, the reason is in the trail, and no message is sent.

stories.name: Show the manager the silent proposals
stories.summary: The manager's view lists proposals past their date with the days of silence per broker.

sections.why: The number only moves when someone sees it weekly.
sections.context: The manager reviews the pipeline on Mondays.
sections.story: As a sales manager, I want silent proposals per broker, so that Monday's review starts from facts.
expected: List sorted by days past the date.
Count per broker; a link to the proposal.
Exported to the weekly digest (BA-CRM-F03).
tech: Query over proposals and activities.

cases.given: a proposal's date was eight days ago with no activity
cases.then: it appears with 8 days and the broker's name.

cases.case: A proposal with activity is not silent
cases.given: a follow-up was sent yesterday
cases.then: the proposal is not listed.

sections.why: Half the pipeline is proposals nobody follows up. A date, a draft and a manager's view turn silence into a list.
sections.problem: Proposals without next steps; reminders ignored; the manager finds out late.
sections.value: More closings from proposals already made; less time chasing.
behavior: Next step and date on creation.
acceptance: No proposal saved without a step and a date.
The draft carries the proposal facts.
The list counts days of silence.
rules: Tier 2 for follow-ups.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Share of drafts approved without edits; days of silence median per week.
open: Whether developer follow-ups go from the broker's mailbox or the brokerage's.

features.name: Counter-proposal preview with the developer's rules
features.summary: Before sending a counter-proposal, the broker sees whether it fits the developer's discount and payment rules, with the rule and its date.

kpi.name: Counter-proposals inside the rules
kpi.definition: Counter-proposals within the developer's discount and payment table ÷ counter-proposals sent
kpi.impact: A counter-proposal outside the rules is a week lost and a buyer told no twice.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Check a counter-proposal against the developer's table
stories.summary: The broker enters the buyer's offer; the assistant shows whether discount, down payment and installments fit the developer's table, rule by rule.

sections.why: Brokers learn the rules by being refused. The table exists; the check should read it.
sections.context: Each developer has a table per project, dated, kept by the back office.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the offer checked against the table before I send it, so that I do not promise what the developer refuses.
expected: Three checks: discount ceiling, minimum down payment, maximum installments.
Each check shows the rule and the table's date.
An offer outside the rules is not blocked; it is flagged with what would make it fit.
tech: Table lookup by project; the preview is read-only.

cases.given: the table allows 5% and the offer asks 8%
cases.then: the discount line is flagged with 'ceiling 5%, table of March 3' and the rest pass.

cases.case: A table that is out of date
cases.given: the project's table is older than 30 days
cases.then: the preview says the table may be stale and names the back office contact.

stories.name: Draft the counter-proposal message from the checked offer
stories.summary: Once the offer fits or the broker accepts the flags, the assistant drafts the message to the developer with the offer and the buyer's facts.

sections.why: The message to the developer is the same every time and still takes twenty minutes.
sections.context: Developer messages go by email with a fixed structure.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the counter-proposal drafted from the checked offer, so that I send a complete message in one go.
expected: Draft with unit, offer, payment plan, buyer qualification facts.
Flags, if accepted, are stated as requests, not hidden.
Sent after approval.
tech: Template plus model for the free text; send through email adapter.

cases.given: the offer passed the checks
cases.then: it carries unit, offer, plan and the four buyer facts.

cases.given: the broker accepted the discount flag
cases.then: the discount is stated as a request to the developer, with the rule quoted.

sections.why: Counter-proposals outside the rules cost a week each. The table exists; the preview makes the broker read it before the developer does.
sections.problem: Rules learned by refusal; stale tables; incomplete messages.
sections.objective: 100% of counter-proposals inside the rules or explicitly flagged.
sections.value: Faster answers from developers; fewer buyers told no twice.
behavior: Three checks with the rule and date.
Drafted message from the checked offer.
acceptance: Flags are stated in the draft.
rules: Never a rule from the conversation; only from the table.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Zero counter-proposals sent with an unflagged rule breach.
open: Who updates the tables and how often (back office decision).

features.name: Proposal status synced from the developer's system
features.summary: The developer's answer to a proposal reaches the CRM within a day, from the developer's export, without the broker retyping it.

kpi.name: Status in sync
kpi.definition: Proposals whose CRM status matches the developer's system ÷ open proposals
kpi.impact: The forecast reads the status; a stale status is a wrong forecast.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Import the developer's proposal export daily
stories.summary: A daily import reads the developer's CSV export and matches each line to a proposal by number and buyer document.

sections.why: Developers answer in their own system; the broker learns by phone. The export is the only honest source.
sections.context: Two developers provide a daily CSV; others are later.
sections.story: The assistant imports the developer export daily and matches lines to proposals, so that status changes can be proposed to the broker.
expected: Match by proposal number, then by buyer document.
Unmatched lines listed for the back office.
No write without a match.
tech: Scheduled import; matching rules; unmatched report.

cases.given: the export has proposal 5521 for buyer document ending 44
cases.then: the line is linked to the proposal and nothing is written yet.

cases.given: the export has a proposal number the CRM does not know
cases.then: the line is in the unmatched report; no proposal is created.

stories.name: Propose the status change to the broker
stories.summary: When the developer's status differs from the CRM, the broker sees a proposed change with the developer's value and date, for approval.

sections.why: A status written without the broker seeing it is the kind of write that breaks trust.
sections.context: Statuses: under analysis, accepted, refused, counter.
sections.story: As a broker, I want status changes proposed with the developer's value, so that I approve what I can explain to the buyer.
expected: Proposed change in the preview with old value, new value and the export's date.
Approve writes; refuse records a reason and keeps the line for the back office.
tech: Preview through BA-CRM-F01; refuse feeds the unmatched report.

cases.given: the export says 'accepted' and the CRM says 'under analysis'
cases.then: the broker sees the proposed change with the date and approves or refuses.

cases.given: the export and the CRM agree
cases.then: nothing is proposed.

stories.name: Measure the sync and its failures
stories.summary: A weekly report shows the share of proposals in sync, the unmatched lines and the time from export to CRM.

sections.why: A sync nobody measures drifts in a month.
sections.context: Report in the manager's digest.
sections.story: As a product manager, I want the sync measured weekly, so that drift is caught before the forecast reads it.
expected: In-sync share, unmatched count, median delay.
Included in the weekly digest.
tech: Query over imports and proposals.

cases.case: The number is in the digest
cases.given: a week of imports ran
cases.then: it shows in-sync share, unmatched lines and median delay.

sections.why: The developer's answer is the fact the forecast needs and the broker learns last. The export is the only honest source, so this track reads it.
sections.problem: Statuses retyped late or never; forecast reads stale statuses.
sections.objective: 95% of proposals in sync within a day.
sections.value: A forecast that reads the developers' answers.
acceptance: The number is in the digest.
rules: Tier 2; matching by number then document.
sections.dependencies: Parallel track: depends on BA-PROP-F01 and BA-CRM-F01 only; runs beside waves 3 and 4 while the developer access is negotiated.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Matching precision on a 50-line golden set: 100% (illustrative).
open: Access agreement with the two developers (commercial director).

sections.why: Half of the proposals in the pipeline have no follow-up for more than a week. The buyer cools, the developer forgets, and the broker finds out when the unit is sold to someone else. Without this Epic the assistant stops at the visit.
sections.problem: Proposals live in the developer's system, in email and in the broker's head. Deadlines pass without anyone noticing.
sections.objective: Every open proposal has a next step with a date, a drafted follow-up when the date arrives, and a status that matches the developer's answer within a day.
metrics: Proposals without a follow-up for seven days: from 48% to under 10% (illustrative).
Proposals with a status that matches the developer's system: 95%.
Counter-proposals inside the developer's discount rules: 100%.
scope: Counter-proposal preview with the developer's rules (BA-PROP-F02).
Proposal status synced from the developer's system (BA-PROP-F03, parallel track).
rules: The assistant never sends a proposal or a counter-proposal; it drafts, the broker sends.
Discount limits come from the developer's table, never from the conversation.
sections.dependencies: BA-CRM-F01 for writes; the developer's system export for BA-PROP-F03.
risks: Risk: a developer's discount table is out of date. Mitigation: the table carries its date and the preview shows it.
Risk: status sync creates duplicates. Mitigation: match by proposal number and buyer document.
governance: The commercial director owns the discount tables.
Weekly reading of silent proposals per broker.
technical: Reminders from the proposal date and the next-step field.
Developer export as CSV in the first release; API later.
Reads and writes go through the assistant's single CRM write path; every write carries author, previous value, proposed value, written value, origin and approval.

epics.name: The broker approves what the assistant writes
epics.summary: Nothing reaches the CRM without the broker seeing it field by field, and everything that was written can be read back later.

features.name: Field-by-field preview and approval
features.summary: Every write the assistant wants to make is shown as old value, new value and origin, and the broker approves field by field.

kpi.name: Writes approved without edits
kpi.definition: Proposed writes approved as proposed ÷ proposed writes
kpi.impact: This number is the trust the brokers put in the assistant, measured.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Create the single write path to the CRM
stories.summary: All CRM writes from the assistant go through one service that records author, previous value, proposed value, written value, origin and approval.

sections.why: Two write paths diverge on the first correction. One path is what makes the trail and the undo possible.
sections.context: The CRM exposes a REST API with field-level writes.
sections.story: The assistant writes to the CRM only through one path that records every write, so that the trail and the undo exist from day one.
expected: One service; no other code calls the CRM write API.
Every write stored with the six attributes.
A write without an approval reference is refused.
tech: Service with a contract table (object, field, allowed values); refusal is an error, not a silent skip.

cases.case: A write without approval is refused
cases.given: a caller sends a write with no approval reference
cases.then: the write is refused and logged as refused.

cases.given: a broker approved a stage change
cases.then: the record carries author, previous, proposed, written value, origin and approval.

stories.name: Show the preview with old and new values
stories.summary: Before a write, the broker sees each field with its old value, the proposed value and the phrase or source it came from, and approves or edits per field.

sections.why: Approval of a block is approval of nothing; the broker has to see each field.
sections.context: Preview in the assistant's chat and in the web app.
sections.story: As a broker, I want each field shown with old, new and source, so that I approve what I understand.
expected: Old value, new value, source per field.
Approve all, approve one, edit one, discard with reason.
Edited values are written as edited, with the original kept.
tech: Rendered from the proposed writes; edits create new proposed values with origin 'broker'.

cases.given: three fields are proposed
cases.then: each shows old, new and source, with its own approve.

cases.case: An edit is recorded as an edit
cases.given: the broker changes the proposed date
cases.then: the written value is the edited one and the trail shows both.

stories.name: Undo any write for 24 hours
stories.summary: The broker can undo any write made through the assistant within 24 hours; the previous value is restored and the undo is recorded.

sections.why: An undo the broker trusts is what lets them approve faster.
sections.context: Undo from the trail or the preview confirmation.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to undo a write within a day, so that approving is not a risk.
expected: Undo restores the previous value through the same write path.
Undo recorded with its reason.
A field changed meanwhile by someone else is not overwritten; the broker is told.
tech: Compare current value with the written value before restoring.

cases.given: a stage was written ten minutes ago
cases.then: the previous stage is restored and the trail shows the undo.

cases.given: the manager changed the stage after the write
cases.then: nothing is overwritten and the broker sees who changed it.

sections.why: No other Feature may write without this one. It is the contract between the assistant and the brokers.
sections.problem: Automatic writes nobody trusts; no audit; no undo.
sections.objective: Every write previewed, approved and reversible.
sections.value: Trust, measured as approvals without edits.
scope: Out: human writes in the CRM itself.
rules: One write path.
Approval per field.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Share of writes approved without edits; reverted writes under 2%.

features.name: Always-allow settings per capability
features.summary: The broker switches each capability of the assistant to always-allow at their own pace, and switches it back with one tap.

kpi.name: Capabilities on always-allow
kpi.definition: Brokers with at least one capability on always-allow ÷ active brokers
kpi.impact: Autonomy earned broker by broker, visible as a number.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Switch a capability to always-allow
stories.summary: In settings, the broker sees each capability with its approval count and error count, and can switch it to always-allow.

sections.why: The setting makes autonomy the broker's decision, with the evidence next to the switch.
sections.context: Capabilities: buyer reminders, visit outcome fields, follow-up drafts.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to switch a capability to always-allow when I trust it, so that I stop approving what I never edit.
expected: Per capability: approvals, edits, undos in the last 30 days next to the switch.
A capability with an undo in the last 7 days cannot be switched on; the reason is shown.
Switching is recorded in the trail.
tech: Settings stored per broker; checked at send or write time.

cases.case: The evidence is next to the switch
cases.given: reminders were approved 20 times with no edit
cases.then: the switch shows 20 approvals, 0 edits, 0 undos and can be turned on.

cases.case: A recent undo blocks the switch
cases.given: an outcome write was undone three days ago
cases.when: the broker tries to switch outcomes to always-allow
cases.then: the switch stays off with 'an undo in the last 7 days'.

stories.name: Pause always-allow with one tap, everywhere
stories.summary: From any message or write made under always-allow, the broker can pause the capability for a day or switch it back to approve-each.

sections.why: Autonomy without a brake is autonomy nobody switches on.
sections.context: Pause from the chat, the app and the digest.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to pause always-allow from where I see the result, so that switching on is safe.
expected: Pause for 24 hours or switch back, from the message itself.
Recorded in the trail with the reason if given.
tech: Setting change through the same settings service.

cases.given: a reminder went out under always-allow
cases.then: the capability is paused for 24 hours and the trail records it.

sections.why: Trust grows unevenly across brokers and capabilities. A per-capability switch, with the evidence next to it, lets each broker widen autonomy at their pace.
sections.problem: Approve-each forever, or automatic for all: both lose brokers.
sections.objective: Half the brokers with one capability on always-allow after a month.
sections.value: Fewer approvals; autonomy that is earned and reversible.
rules: Per broker, per capability.
Irreversible actions stay at approve-each.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Undo rate under always-allow compared with approve-each.
open: Whether the manager sees each broker's switches (privacy decision).

features.name: Activity trail and daily digest
features.summary: Everything the assistant did on a record can be read back, and each broker receives a daily digest of what was written in their name.

kpi.name: Writes approved without edits
kpi.definition: Proposed writes approved as proposed ÷ proposed writes
kpi.impact: The trail is where the number is read; the digest is where the broker sees it.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Show the trail on the record
stories.summary: On any lead, visit or proposal, a trail lists what the assistant proposed, what the broker approved or edited, and when, in plain sentences.

sections.why: A write someone cannot read back is a write someone will dispute.
sections.context: Trail in the CRM record and in the app.
sections.story: As a broker, I want to read what the assistant did on a record, so that I can explain it to the buyer and the manager.
expected: One line per write: field, old, new, who approved, when.
Grouped per day.
Links to the source phrase when it exists.
out: Trails for human writes made directly in the CRM.
tech: Rendered from the write log.

cases.case: A write reads as a sentence
cases.given: the stage changed from visit to proposal on Tuesday
cases.then: it reads 'stage: visit to proposal, approved by you, Tuesday 16:10, from the visit outcome'.

stories.name: Send the daily digest
stories.summary: At 18:30 each broker receives an email with what was written in their name that day, what is waiting for approval and what is silent.

sections.why: The digest is the daily contract: nothing happened that the broker did not see by evening.
sections.context: Email; the manager's digest is a separate story.
sections.story: As a broker, I want a daily digest of what was written and what waits, so that I end the day knowing.
expected: Three blocks: written today, waiting for approval, silent items.
Empty blocks are stated as empty.
Sent at 18:30; nothing sent on days with nothing.
tech: Scheduled job; email adapter.

cases.given: two writes were made and one preview waits
cases.then: the digest lists the two writes and the waiting preview.

cases.given: no write, no waiting preview, no silent item
cases.then: no email is sent.

sections.why: Trust is read back, not declared. The trail and the digest are where the broker verifies the assistant every day.
sections.problem: No audit; surprises discovered weeks later.
sections.objective: Every write readable on the record and summarized daily.
sections.value: Disputes end in a minute; the manager reads the same facts.
acceptance: One line per write with the five facts.
Digest sent only when there is content.
rules: The trail is stored with the write, never reconstructed.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Digest open rate; disputes per month.

sections.why: An assistant that writes to the CRM on its own is an assistant the brokers switch off. Without this Epic every other Epic has no write path and no trust.
sections.problem: Brokers do not trust automatic updates; managers cannot audit what changed; the CRM has fields nobody owns.
sections.objective: A preview-and-approve step for every write, settings that let each broker widen the assistant's autonomy at their own pace, and a trail that explains every change.
metrics: Writes approved without edits: a measured baseline, then 80% after two months (illustrative).
Writes reverted within a day: under 2%.
Brokers who switched a capability to always-allow after the first month: 50%.
rules: One write path. Every write carries author, previous value, proposed value, written value, origin and approval.
Always-allow is per capability and per broker, never global.
Undo is available for 24 hours on any write.

risks: Risk: the preview adds friction and brokers skip it. Mitigation: one screen, one approve button, and always-allow once trust is earned.
Risk: the trail becomes noise. Mitigation: grouped per record and per day.
governance: Autonomy tiers follow the eval results per capability, decided monthly by the product manager and the sales manager.
technical: A write service with a contract table (object, field, allowed values).
Trail stored with the write, never reconstructed.
Digest by email, daily, per broker.

epics.name: The forecast matches the evidence
epics.summary: The stage and the forecast category of each deal follow what happened in visits and proposals, with the reason written next to them.

features.name: Stage suggestion with its reason
features.summary: After a visit outcome or a proposal event, the assistant proposes the deal's stage with the reason, for the broker's approval.

kpi.name: Stage matches the evidence
kpi.definition: Deals whose stage matches the last recorded event ÷ open deals
kpi.impact: A pipeline whose stages match the events is a pipeline the manager can read.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Propose the stage from the last event
stories.summary: A rule table maps events to stages: first reply, visit held, proposal made, developer answer. After each event the stage is proposed with the rule as the reason.

sections.why: Stages move on hope today; the rule table moves them on events.
sections.context: Five stages agreed with the commercial director.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the stage proposed from what happened, with the rule shown, so that I approve a fact.
expected: Rule table with event, stage and reason text.
Proposal through the preview, with the event linked.
No stage goes backwards without the broker's explicit choice.
tech: Rules; the preview is BA-CRM-F01's.

cases.case: A visit held proposes the stage
cases.given: a visit outcome was recorded
cases.then: the stage 'visited' is proposed with 'visit held on April 2' as the reason.

cases.given: the proposal was refused by the developer
cases.then: the assistant proposes 'counter or close' and never 'lead'.

stories.name: Flag a stage changed without an event
stories.summary: A stage changed by hand with no event behind it is flagged to the manager with the broker's reason, not blocked.

sections.why: Flagging keeps the broker's freedom and gives the manager the exception list.
sections.context: Manual stage changes happen in the CRM.
sections.story: As a sales manager, I want stages changed without an event listed with the reason, so that I review exceptions, not everything.
expected: Flag with broker, deal, old and new stage, reason.
Listed in the manager's weekly digest.
tech: Compare stage changes with the event log.

cases.given: the broker moved a deal to 'proposal' with no proposal recorded
cases.then: the change is listed with the reason the broker typed, or 'no reason'.

sections.why: The events created by the other Epics are worth nothing to the forecast until they move the stage. This Feature moves it, with the reason written.
sections.objective: 90% of stages matching the last event.
sections.value: A pipeline the manager can read without asking.
rules: Rules first; a model only for the reason text.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Agreement with the manager's manual review on 40 deals: 90% (illustrative).
open: Stage definitions in the glossary (commercial director).

features.name: Forecast category from evidence
features.summary: The forecast category (commit, likely, possible) is proposed from the stage, the qualification score and the proposal status, with the reason.

kpi.name: Forecast accuracy
kpi.definition: Deals closed in the month ÷ deals in commit and likely at the start of the month
kpi.impact: The number the company runs on, finally read from evidence.
kpi.source: the assistant's own event log and the CRM mirror, read weekly

stories.name: Propose the category with its three inputs
stories.summary: The category is proposed from stage, score and proposal status, and the preview shows the three inputs and the rule.

sections.why: A category with its inputs visible is a category two people can discuss.
sections.context: Three categories, defined by the commercial director.
sections.story: As a broker, I want the category proposed with its inputs, so that the manager and I argue about facts.
expected: Rule table: stage × score × status to category.
Preview with the three inputs.
The broker can keep their own category with a reason, recorded.
tech: Rules; preview through BA-CRM-F01.

cases.given: stage 'proposal', score 4, status 'under analysis'
cases.then: category 'likely' is proposed with the three inputs shown.

cases.given: the broker keeps 'commit' with a reason
cases.then: the category is 'commit', the reason is in the trail, and the manager sees the disagreement.

stories.name: Show the manager the forecast with its reasons
stories.summary: The manager's forecast view lists deals by category with the reason and the disagreements, and the month-end accuracy once closings are known.

sections.why: The weekly forecast meeting is where this program is judged.
sections.context: Monday review; month-end closing data from the developers.
sections.story: As a sales manager, I want the forecast by category with reasons and the accuracy at month end, so that the meeting reads evidence.
expected: Deals by category with reason and disagreement flag.
Month-end accuracy per category, computed from closings.
Exported to the manager's weekly digest.
tech: Query over deals, categories and closings.

cases.given: ten deals are in 'likely'
cases.then: each shows its reason and whether the broker disagreed.

cases.given: closings for March are known
cases.then: accuracy per category for March is shown next to February's.

stories.name: Evaluate the category rules against closings
stories.summary: Each month the rules are scored against actual closings on the previous months' deals, and the product manager sees which rule misfires.

sections.why: Rules that are never scored are opinions with a table.
sections.context: Monthly, after closings are imported.
sections.story: As a product manager, I want the category rules scored monthly, so that the table changes on evidence.
expected: Per rule: deals, closings, accuracy.
A rule below 60% for two months is flagged for review.
tech: Query over history; report in the product manager's view.

cases.given: February closings are in
cases.then: each rule shows deals, closings and accuracy, and the ones under 60% twice are flagged.

sections.why: The category is the number the company runs on. Proposed from three visible inputs, it becomes a fact two people can discuss instead of a hope one person defends.
sections.problem: Categories mean different things per broker; accuracy unknown.
sections.objective: Plus 15 points of accuracy after the baseline.
sections.value: A forecast meeting that reads evidence.
rules: Rules first.
The broker may disagree with a reason.
nfr: Preview opens in under two seconds on a phone.
Every write is logged with its origin.
evaluation: Monthly rule accuracy; flag under 60% twice.

sections.why: The manager's forecast is a weekly negotiation between what brokers hope and what the CRM shows. Without this Epic the data the other Epics create never reaches the number the company runs on.
sections.problem: Stages are updated late and optimistically; forecast categories mean different things to different brokers.
sections.objective: A stage suggestion with its reason after every visit and proposal event, and a forecast category derived from evidence, both approved by the broker.
metrics: Deals whose stage matches the last recorded event: from 55% to 90% (illustrative).
Forecast accuracy at month end, measured against closings: a baseline, then plus 15 points.
rules: The assistant suggests; the broker decides; the manager sees the reason.
A category change without an event is flagged, not blocked.
sections.dependencies: BA-VISIT-F02 and BA-PROP-F03 for the events; BA-CRM-F01 for the writes.
risks: Risk: brokers feel policed. Mitigation: the reason is shown to the broker first, and the manager sees categories, not brokers' edits.
governance: The commercial director owns the category definitions, written in the glossary.
technical: Rules first; a model only for the reason text.
Reads and writes go through the assistant's single CRM write path; every write carries author, previous value, proposed value, written value, origin and approval.

improvements.name: Show the time since arrival in minutes under one hour, hours after
improvements.summary: The queue showed '0 h' for a lead that arrived 40 minutes ago; brokers read it as fresh.

improvements.name: Keep the draft's original when the broker edits
improvements.summary: Brokers asked to see what the assistant wrote before their edit, to decide whether to keep editing.

improvements.name: A lead with two phone numbers was imported twice
improvements.summary: Seen on 2026-04-02 on a portal lead with a landline and a mobile number. Both records show the same message. Origin of the second number to be verified with the portal.

improvements.name: The preview showed the old value of a field changed by the broker a minute before
improvements.summary: Seen on 2026-04-08. The preview read the record before the broker's own edit was saved. Expected: the preview reads the current value. The source of the read to be verified.

asks.ask: Let the assistant answer the fee and parking questions without me when the catalogue has them.
asks.note: Depends on always-allow for first replies, which stays off until the eval set passes.

asks.ask: Propose a visit slot in the first reply.
asks.note: Open item in BA-LEAD-F02; decision with BA-VISIT-F03.

asks.ask: Record the visit outcome from the stand's tablet, not only from my phone.
asks.note: Needs the stand devices; no estimate.

asks.ask: A weekly digest for managers with silent proposals and exceptions.
asks.note: Fed by BA-PROP-F01-US03 and BA-FCST-F01-US02; the digest itself is a later Feature.

glossary.def: A per-broker, per-capability setting that lets the assistant act without approving each action.
The brokerage's list of units with price, conditions and stand hours, kept by the back office and dated.
Commit, likely or possible: how sure the company is that a deal closes this month.
The company that builds and sells the launch; it sets discount and payment rules and answers proposals.
A story that builds something the other stories need and that no broker sees directly. It has no persona.
A fixed set of real, anonymized inputs with the expected result, used to score a probabilistic behavior.
A buyer who wrote about a listing through a portal or walked in.
A behavior with zero tolerance, scored separately: an invented price, a write without approval.
Fibonacci story points (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) set by the developer who will build the story; 0 means not estimated.
The screen where a proposed write shows old value, new value and source, per field, before the broker approves.
Where a deal is: lead, visited, proposal, counter or close, closed.
The developer's sales office at the launch, with its own opening hours.
The list of what the assistant proposed and the broker approved on a record, stored with each write.
A delivery group that ends with something a broker uses in production; the order dependencies may not cross.
The single service through which every write to the CRM passes, recording six attributes.
